titulo.en: I hope they accept me in Madrid

objetivo.en: Express a wish about something you don't know yet with ojalá + present subjunctive.

traduccion.en: I hope; hopefully; if only

nota.en: Say “oh-hah-LAH”: the j is a strong h and the stress is on the last syllable. It comes from Arabic and once meant “God willing”. It never changes form.

traduccion.en: the admission, the acceptance

nota.en: Say “ahd-mee-SYOHN”. Stress the last syllable.

traduccion.en: the application, the request

nota.en: Say “soh-lee-see-TOOD”. It is not “solicitude”: la solicitud is the form or request you send.

traduccion.en: the letter of recommendation

nota.en: Say “reh-koh-mehn-dah-SYOHN”. Plural: las cartas de recomendación.

traduccion.en: the (academic) record, the file

nota.en: Say “ehks-peh-DYEHN-teh”. Here it means the file of your grades and documents.

traduccion.en: the master's degree, the master's program

nota.en: Say “mah-ehs-TREE-ah”. The accent mark shows the stress on the í.

traduccion.en: the applicant, the candidate

nota.en: Say “ahs-pee-RAHN-teh”. It is the same for men and women: el aspirante, la aspirante.

traduccion.en: to accept

nota.en: Say “ah-sehp-TAR”: the c before e sounds like s. For a person, use a: me aceptan = they accept me.

traduccion.en: to long for, to yearn for

nota.en: Say “ah-neh-LAR”: the h is silent. It is a strong, literary way to say “to want very much”.

traduccion.en: the wish, the desire

nota.en: Say “deh-SEH-oh”. Related verb: desear, to wish.

explicacion.en: English speakers say “I hope they accept me” with the ordinary present. After ojalá Spanish needs the present subjunctive: acepten.
Ojalá does not change, but the verb after it must be in the subjunctive and match the person: tengas for tú.
A negative wish also uses the subjunctive: ojalá no llueva. Do not keep the indicative llueve.
English “I hope to pass” uses an infinitive, so it is tempting to say ojalá aprobar. After ojalá use a conjugated subjunctive verb: apruebe, apruebes, aprueben…

texto.en: English says “I hope you pass” with the ordinary present. Spanish uses the single word ojalá and then the present subjunctive: Ojalá apruebes el examen. Ojalá means “I hope” or “hopefully”, and it never changes: it is the same for yo, tú, él or ustedes. Only the verb after it changes to match the person who will do the action: Ojalá me acepten en Madrid (I hope they accept me). Why the subjunctive? Because you do not know yet whether it will happen: it is a wish, not a fact. You already know this tool from desires with que (Quiero que vengas); ojalá is the short version. You can also say ojalá que, with the same meaning: Ojalá que tengas suerte.

To hope that something does not happen, put no right after ojalá: Ojalá no llueva el sábado. Do not use the indicative (llueve) or the infinitive: Ojalá no llueva, never Ojalá no llueve. Review the very common irregular subjunctive forms you already know: ser → sea, estar → esté, ir → vaya, tener → tenga, poder → pueda, hacer → haga. Verbs that change the stem keep the change: aprobar → apruebes, poder → puedas, pedir → pidan. Dar is irregular too: te den, me den (they give you, they give me).

explicacion.en: English speakers translate “must be at home” with ser. For place and state use the future of estar: estará en casa.
Hours are plural, as in son las diez, so the guess is serán las diez. Only la una is singular: será la una.
Tener has an irregular future stem: tendr-. Do not add the endings to the infinitive tener.
English uses the same verb “is” for everything, but Spanish uses estar for a state such as being asleep: está dormido. A guess about it is estará dormido.

titulo.en: The future for guesses about now

texto.en: In English you guess about the present with “must be” or “probably”: “He must be asleep”, “It's probably nine o'clock”. Spanish often uses the future tense for the same idea: Estará dormido. Serán las nueve. Here the future does not mean tomorrow. It means “I guess it is so right now”. You already know how to build the future (hablaré, tendré, estaré), so only the meaning is new. You can also ask yourself the question: ¿Dónde estará Mateo? (I wonder where Mateo is.) ¿Qué hora será? (I wonder what time it is.) The speaker is not asking the other person for facts; they are thinking aloud.

Compare Mañana llegará a las ocho (a real future: tomorrow) and Ahora llegará tarde (a guess about the present). The time word helps: mañana points to the future, while ahora, ya or a question about the present points to a guess. The irregular future stems stay the same: tendrá (tener), hará (hacer), sabrá (saber), habrá (haber), podrá (poder), dirá (decir). For serán with hours, the verb is plural, like son las diez: Serán las diez. With la una it is singular: Será la una. To say “most likely” you can add seguramente, and to sound very sure, sin duda. You can also say supongo que + present: Supongo que está dormido.

erroresFrecuentes.correcto: A lo mejor llueve el sábado.

explicacion.en: English has one word, “maybe”, for everything. In Spanish a lo mejor takes the indicative. Use the subjunctive only with quizás and tal vez.
A lo mejor is not followed by que. Say the verb directly: a lo mejor llueve, a lo mejor vamos.
Ir is irregular in the subjunctive: vaya, vayas, vaya. Do not build it from voy.
After quizás and tal vez you need a conjugated verb in the subjunctive, not an infinitive: pueda, vaya, venga. English “maybe not to be able to go” should not be translated word for word.

texto.en: Spanish has two groups of “maybe” expressions, and each takes a different mood. A lo mejor takes the ordinary indicative, the same one you use for facts: A lo mejor llueve. A lo mejor vamos. Quizás and tal vez take the subjunctive in this course: Quizás llueva. Tal vez no pueda ir. All of them mean “maybe” or “perhaps”, and the speaker is not sure. Native speakers sometimes use the indicative after quizás and tal vez too, but the subjunctive is the standard choice and it is always correct, so use it. Never mix the two groups: you cannot say a lo mejor llueva.

After quizás and tal vez, the subjunctive forms you already know appear again: vaya (ir), sea (ser), esté (estar), sepa (saber), haga (hacer), venga (venir), tenga (tener), pueda (poder). With nosotros, the subjunctive of ir is vayamos and of tener is tengamos. The expression can go before the verb, as in Quizás llueva, or the subject can come in between: Quizás Daniela también vaya. In a negative sentence, no goes right before the verb: Tal vez no pueda ir. With a lo mejor, the sentence is just like an ordinary statement: A lo mejor comemos en casa.

explicacion.en: English “should have studied” can tempt you to use the infinitive. After haber you always need the participle: estudiado.
Hacer has an irregular participle: hecho. The same happens with decir → dicho, escribir → escrito, poner → puesto and ver → visto.
The pronoun goes at the end of haber, not after the participle: haberla llamado, haberte escrito.
Deber + infinitive gives advice for now or the future. To talk about a past regret, use haber + participle: deberías haberla llamado ayer.

titulo.en: Debería haber + participle: regret about the past

texto.en: In English “I should have studied” looks back at the past. Spanish builds it with debería + haber + participle: Debería haber estudiado más. Deber changes with the person (debería, deberías, debería, deberíamos, deberían), but haber stays in the infinitive and the participle never changes for gender or number: Deberías haber llamado a Rosa. Compare the two ideas. Deberías + infinitive gives advice for now: Deberías llamarla ahora. Deberías haber + participle looks at the past: Deberías haberla llamado ayer. It says that the action did not happen, and now you wish it had. It can express regret about yourself or a mild criticism of another person.

titulo.en: Negative sentences, pronouns and irregular participles

texto.en: To say that something was a mistake, put no before debería: No debería haber dicho eso (I shouldn't have said that). Object pronouns attach to the end of haber: Debería haberla llamado (I should have called her), Debería haberte escrito (I should have written to you). A common mistake is to put the pronoun after the participle, as in haber llamado la. The regular participles end in -ado or -ido: estudiado, salido, esperado. Review these irregular ones: hacer → hecho, decir → dicho, escribir → escrito, poner → puesto, ver → visto. Spanish does not use hacido or decido.

explicacion.en: After no estoy segura de que, Spanish uses the subjunctive because you have doubts: sea. Do not keep the indicative es.
Dudar expresses doubt, so the verb after que is in the subjunctive: sepa.

erroresFrecuentes.correcto: Estoy segura de que es de Rosa.

explicacion.en: When you are sure, use the indicative. The subjunctive is only for doubt, so after estoy segura de que say es.

texto.en: To say how sure you are, Spanish changes the mood of the verb. When you are certain, you state a fact, so you use the indicative: Estoy segura de que es de Rosa. When you have doubts, the idea is not confirmed, so you use the subjunctive: No estoy segura de que sea de Mateo. Dudar (to doubt) works like “not sure”: Dudo que lo sepa. Notice the small word de. In English you can say “I'm sure that…”, but in Spanish the phrase is estar seguro de que. Seguro changes with the speaker: seguro (man), segura (woman). You already know the same pattern from creo que + indicative and no creo que + subjunctive.

When you ask whether someone is sure of a fact, you stay with the indicative: ¿Estás segura de que viene? Here you are asking about a fact that you expect to be true or false, not saying you doubt it. Compare the pairs in the table: certainty on the left, doubt on the right. The verbs you need most are the ones you already know: sea (ser), esté (estar), venga (venir), sepa (saber), tenga (tener), haga (hacer), pueda (poder). If you just want to guess, you can also use the tools from earlier classes: quizás, a lo mejor and the future of probability, such as ¿Quién será?

feedback.en: Model: Estoy segura de que la bolsa no es de Mateo, porque él siempre avisa antes de venir. No estoy segura de que sea de tu mamá, pero quizás ella tenga algo rico para nosotras. Dudo que sea del casero porque nunca nos trae nada.
